docs.text: Coupling design The SUMMA--mizuRoute integration supports two different workflows for combining land-surface simulations with river-network routing: Sequential: SUMMA and mizuRoute are run as separate executables. SUMMA first generates runoff, which is subsequently provided as input to a standalone mizuRoute simulation. Coupled: mizuRoute is linked directly with SUMMA and river routing is performed during the SUMMA simulation. The sequential workflow remains useful when land-surface and river-routing simulations can be performed independently. The coupled workflow allows information to be exchanged between the land and river components during model execution. This capability is needed for applications such as streamflow data assimilation and, more generally, coupling between terrestrial and river processes. Design philosophy The SUMMA--mizuRoute integration was designed around a simple principle: mizuRoute provides river-network routing capabilities, while the host land model controls the overall coupled simulation. In a standalone mizuRoute simulation, mizuRoute manages the complete routing workflow. It reads runoff generated by a land model, initializes the river network, manages its parallel execution, performs river-network routing, and writes the resulting streamflow and other routing variables to its own output files. In a coupled simulation, these responsibilities are deliberately divided between mizuRoute and the host land model. The host model manages the overall simulation, including the model driver, data exchange, and I/O. mizuRoute provides the specialized capabilities needed to initialize the river network and perform the routing calculations. The coupled implementation therefore separates these routing capabilities from the infrastructure used to run mizuRoute as a standalone model. Initialization and river-network routing are exposed as distinct operations that can be invoked by the host model. The host model determines when these operations are performed, supplies the required runoff and other information, and manages the resulting routed quantities within its own simulation framework. For SUMMA, this means that SUMMA retains control of its model driver, data structures, and NetCDF I/O, while mizuRoute remains responsible for constructing the river network and performing the river-routing calculations. This avoids requiring SUMMA to adopt the execution and I/O infrastructure of the standalone mizuRoute model. This design is intended to make mizuRoute a reusable routing component rather than a routing system tied specifically to SUMMA. Other land surface or hydrologic models can adopt the same pattern: the host model manages the coupled simulation and calls a small number of mizuRoute operations to initialize and route the river network. The SUMMA implementation therefore provides one example of a more general coupling strategy rather than a SUMMA-specific design. Parallel execution The intended parallel design described above has not yet been implemented in the current SUMMA--mizuRoute coupling. At present, the coupled configuration does not support parallel execution of the coupled land--river system. SUMMA has an existing domain-parallel implementation in which the land-model domain is divided into spatial chunks that can be simulated independently. This strategy works because the land calculations in different domain partitions do not normally require exchange of model states between partitions. River-network routing introduces a fundamentally different dependency structure. Flow generated in one part of the domain must be propagated downstream through the connected river network. Upstream and downstream reaches can occur in different SUMMA domain partitions, so those partitions can no longer be advanced independently. The existing SUMMA domain decomposition therefore cannot simply be applied to the coupled land--river system. The long-term design is for the host model to extend its parallel execution strategy to account explicitly for river-network connectivity. The host model would coordinate the exchange of information across domain partitions while mizuRoute would continue to provide the network topology and routing calculations. This preserves the broader design principle that the host model controls execution of the coupled system rather than requiring it to adopt the parallel execution infrastructure of the standalone mizuRoute model. Developing this capability requires a decomposition and communication strategy that respects both the land-model partitioning and dependencies along the river network. Parallelization of the coupled SUMMA--mizuRoute system therefore remains future work. Until this capability is implemented, users who require the parallel routing capabilities currently available in mizuRoute should use the sequential workflow : first run SUMMA to generate runoff and then run the standalone mizuRoute executable using its native parallel implementation. Software independence and portability An important objective of the coupling design is to preserve the independence of SUMMA and mizuRoute. Both models remain usable as standalone modeling systems, and coupling should not require either model to incorporate the internal implementation details of the other. mizuRoute is included in SUMMA as a Git submodule, allowing SUMMA to use a specific upstream mizuRoute release while maintaining a clear boundary between the two codebases. The current implementation is tied to mizuRoute v3.1.1 , and no source files within that Git submodule have been modified for the SUMMA coupling. All SUMMA-specific integration code is maintained outside the mizuRoute submodule. The coupling is deliberately restricted to a small number of exchanges between the host model and mizuRoute. Keeping this interface narrow reduces dependencies between the two codebases and makes it easier for each model to evolve independently. This separation is also important for portability. A coupling architecture that depends extensively on SUMMA data structures, execution logic, or I/O would be difficult to reproduce in another land model. In contrast, an interface based on a small number of initialization, data-exchange, and routing operations can be implemented by another host model with relatively little modification. The goal is therefore not simply to couple mizuRoute to SUMMA, but to establish a pattern in which mizuRoute can provide river-routing capabilities to different host modeling systems while allowing each host model to retain control of its own simulation infrastructure. The technical implementation of this design, including the thin interface layer, compatibility shims, coupling points, and management of source dependencies in CMake, is described in Coupling architecture .

docs.text: Running mizuRoute mizuRoute can be run with SUMMA using either the sequential or coupled configuration described in Coupling design . Sequential configuration In the sequential configuration, SUMMA and mizuRoute are run as separate executables. SUMMA is run first to generate runoff, and the resulting SUMMA NetCDF output is subsequently used as input to standalone mizuRoute. Configuration of a standalone mizuRoute simulation is described in the mizuRoute documentation . The standalone simulation is controlled using the standard mizuRoute control file. For example, a control file for a SUMMA--mizuRoute application specifies the simulation period and routing method, the river-network topology, and the SUMMA NetCDF file and variable containing the runoff supplied to mizuRoute. It also specifies whether runoff must be remapped between the SUMMA spatial units and the river-network catchments. Once the mizuRoute control file has been prepared, the standalone model can be run with: mpirun -np <n> route_runoff <mizuRoute_control_file> where <n> is the number of MPI processes, route_runoff is the standalone mizuRoute executable, and <mizuRoute_control_file> is the mizuRoute control file. For example: mpirun -np 4 route_runoff settings/mizuRoute/mizuroute.control Users should refer to the mizuRoute documentation for details of the standalone control file, model options, and parallel execution. Coupled configuration In the coupled configuration, mizuRoute is executed directly within the SUMMA simulation. SUMMA is run normally, with an additional TOML configuration file provided using the -c or --config command-line option. For example: summa.exe \ -m <summa_control_file> \ -c <summa_config_file> The existing SUMMA control file specified with -m is unchanged. The additional configuration file specified with -c currently contains the information required to initialize and run mizuRoute. The TOML configuration is currently used primarily to provide the additional information required by mizuRoute. The longer-term plan is to migrate SUMMA control information to TOML, as described in Coupling architecture . An example configuration is: # mizuRoute control file [mizuRoute] namelist_path = "settings/mizuRoute/" namelist_file = "param.nml.default" methods = "3" dt = 3600 [hydrofabric] hfabric_path = "settings/mizuRoute/" hfabric_file = "topology.nc" dname_seg = "seg" dname_hru = "hru" varname_HRUid = "hruId" varname_segId = "segId" varname_hruSegId = "hruToSegId" varname_downSegId = "downSegId" varname_area = "area" varname_slope = "slope" varname_length = "length" The [mizuRoute] section defines the routing configuration. It specifies the mizuRoute parameter namelist, the routing method or methods to execute, and the routing time step. The [hydrofabric] section identifies the river-network topology file and defines the dimension and variable names used to describe the river network, including: river reaches and hydrologic response units; HRU and reach identifiers; the reach associated with each HRU; downstream reach connectivity; and catchment area, channel slope, and channel length. The methods option identifies the mizuRoute routing method to use. In the example above, methods = "3" selects the Eulerian kinematic-wave routing method. See the mizuRoute documentation for descriptions of the available routing methods. The dt option specifies the mizuRoute routing time step in seconds. In the example above, dt = 3600 specifies an hourly routing time step. The routing time step must be less than or equal to the SUMMA model time step. Coupled output mizuRoute output is written directly into the SUMMA NetCDF output files. The coupled configuration adds a seg dimension for river reaches and a method dimension for the routing method. Routed streamflow is written as: q_reach(time, seg, method) where q_reach is streamflow at the downstream end of each river reach, with units of m3 s-1. The seg coordinate contains the river-reach identifiers, and upArea(seg) provides the drainage area above the downstream end of each reach. Unlike the sequential configuration, the coupled configuration does not require a mizuRoute runoff-input file. SUMMA passes the simulated runoff directly to mizuRoute during model execution. Routed streamflow is written into the SUMMA NetCDF output rather than to a separate standalone mizuRoute output file. Parallel execution The current coupled SUMMA--mizuRoute configuration does not support parallel execution of the coupled land--river system. Users who require mizuRoute's parallel routing capabilities should use the sequential configuration and run the standalone mizuRoute executable using MPI. The reasons for this current limitation, and the intended approach for parallelization of the coupled system, are described in Coupling design .

docs.text: In the coupled configuration, mizuRoute is executed directly within the SUMMA simulation. SUMMA is run normally, with an additional TOML configuration file provided using the -c or --config command-line option. For example: summa.exe \ -m <summa_control_file> \ -c <summa_config_file> The existing SUMMA control file specified with -m is unchanged. The additional configuration file specified with -c currently contains the information required to initialize and run mizuRoute. The TOML configuration is currently used primarily to provide the additional information required by mizuRoute. The longer-term plan is to migrate SUMMA control information to TOML, as described in Coupling architecture . An example configuration is: # mizuRoute control file [mizuRoute] namelist_path = "settings/mizuRoute/" namelist_file = "param.nml.default" methods = "3" dt = 3600 [hydrofabric] hfabric_path = "settings/mizuRoute/" hfabric_file = "topology.nc" dname_seg = "seg" dname_hru = "hru" varname_HRUid = "hruId" varname_segId = "segId" varname_hruSegId = "hruToSegId" varname_downSegId = "downSegId" varname_area = "area" varname_slope = "slope" varname_length = "length" The [mizuRoute] section defines the routing configuration. It specifies the mizuRoute parameter namelist, the routing method or methods to execute, and the routing time step. The [hydrofabric] section identifies the river-network topology file and defines the dimension and variable names used to describe the river network, including: river reaches and hydrologic response units; HRU and reach identifiers; the reach associated with each HRU; downstream reach connectivity; and catchment area, channel slope, and channel length. The methods option identifies the mizuRoute routing method to use. In the example above, methods = "3" selects the Eulerian kinematic-wave routing method. See the mizuRoute documentation for descriptions of the available routing methods. The dt option specifies the mizuRoute routing time step in seconds. In the example above, dt = 3600 specifies an hourly routing time step. The routing time step must be less than or equal to the SUMMA model time step.

docs.text: mizuRoute output is written directly into the SUMMA NetCDF output files. The coupled configuration adds a seg dimension for river reaches and a method dimension for the routing method. Routed streamflow is written as: q_reach(time, seg, method) where q_reach is streamflow at the downstream end of each river reach, with units of m3 s-1. The seg coordinate contains the river-reach identifiers, and upArea(seg) provides the drainage area above the downstream end of each reach. Unlike the sequential configuration, the coupled configuration does not require a mizuRoute runoff-input file. SUMMA passes the simulated runoff directly to mizuRoute during model execution. Routed streamflow is written into the SUMMA NetCDF output rather than to a separate standalone mizuRoute output file.

docs.text: The current coupled SUMMA--mizuRoute configuration does not support parallel execution of the coupled land--river system. Users who require mizuRoute's parallel routing capabilities should use the sequential configuration and run the standalone mizuRoute executable using MPI. The reasons for this current limitation, and the intended approach for parallelization of the coupled system, are described in Coupling design .
